title: Edge Walker
context: Grade 4, and the first topic in the chapter that measures anything. An adult sees sides being added up, which any child with a pencil can do. What is actually being taught is that the perimeter is every side of the boundary, including a side the figure does not label. One printed figure, an L-shape, leaves a side unlabelled, and a child who adds only the numbers printed on it is out by the whole of that side. The page never shows how to find such a side, but its own fully labelled stepped figures show the rule: the sides running one way along one side of a stepped shape add up to the side facing them.

writeup.why: Walk all the way round a figure adding every side once, and find any side that is missing before the walk can finish.
writeup.look: A figure with its sides labelled, a small walker at one corner, a string coiled beside it, and a running sum at the top left of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Edge Walker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the running sum, the one number this tool builds: the lengths of the sides walked so far added in ink, climbing by one side's length at each step, with the sides walked against the sides of the figure written small beside it, so a skipped side shows. On the fourth phase it carries the given sides taken off against the sides given, and the length left is read in the bay, not here. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The figure board fills the left of the working area, 700 by 440 at 64,214, with one figure drawn to scale in deep blue, each side's length written in amber beside it in centimetres or metres, and a side with no label carrying an empty amber label box at its true length. The walker, a small round vermilion marker, stands at one corner, and each tap sends it along one side, which lights amber as it goes while its length drops into the running sum. The string lies coiled at the foot of the board, and the string control lays it tight round the whole boundary, lifts it off and straightens it along a near-black ruler 700 by 56 at 64,666, where it reaches a mark that can be set beside the sum. Labelling one side of a rectangle lights the side opposite it with the same length. The facing-sides bracket stands at the right, 370 by 220 at 780,214, and works on a stepped shape whose corners are all square. It takes the sides that run the same way as the missing one along one side of the shape, lays them end to end as amber bars in one row with the missing side as an empty bar, and lays the long side facing them as one bar in the row beneath, both rows starting from the same near-black line, so the missing length is the space left at the end of the top row. Sides running the other way dim while it works. The missing-side bay stands under the bracket, 370 by 200 at 780,450: it lays the perimeter written in a figure's middle as one long amber bar and takes the given sides off it one at a time as bars laid end to end along it, until one length is left. The times-four key sits at 780,666, 180 by 56, and lights only on a figure whose four sides are all equal; pressed, it writes the four equal sides added one under another beside the product, so the adding it replaces is never hidden. The opposite-sides control sits beside it, 180 by 56 at 970,666. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across on every phase, because every answer here is a length. A unit tag under the slot reads centimetres or metres, whichever the figure carries, and is filled in with the number, never left off. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. Every figure is drawn to scale with its labels, and every stepped figure closes up exactly, so wherever one long side faces a run of shorter ones, the shorter ones add up to it, across and upright alike. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries only lengths that can make one, such as three, four and five. A side with no label is drawn at its true length, so it can be seen before it is known.
writeup.finish: The card shows the figure the child walked round, every side labelled, the one they found lit, and the sum standing beside the straightened string.

phases.win: the walker gets home, the sum stops at the perimeter, and the straightened string reaches the same mark on the ruler
phases.does: lights the opposite sides, walks the walker round side by side, then lays the string
phases.goal: the perimeter is every side of the boundary added once
phases.says: Walk all the way round. Add each side as you go. Does the string agree?
phases.check: Away from the screen: measure the length and breadth of a book, and find how far it is all the way round.
phases.feels: the walk goes round once, and every side takes one turn in the sum
phases.hands: Measure a desk's length and breadth with a ruler and write both on the board. Ask how far it is all the way round. A child lays a string round the desk's edge, marks where it meets itself and straightens it against a metre scale. Then add all four sides, each once, and compare the sum with the string.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many sides has the figure? Second rung, the phase's: which sides has the walker not walked yet? Third rung: the figure is cut to a small rectangle, three by two, and the walker goes round it before the larger figure comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: only two numbers are printed on the figure, and adding every number that is printed feels like adding every side.
wrong.move: adds only the two labelled sides of the rectangle, giving forty for a frame twenty-five by fifteen.
wrong.screen: the walker walks the first two sides and the sum stands at forty with the walker only half way round, at the opposite corner. The opposite-sides control lights the two unlabelled sides with the same lengths, the walker walks on, and the sum reaches eighty as it gets home. The child's forty stays in the slot beside the half way mark.

wrong.why: the squares are the plainest things on squared paper to count, and both numbers come off the same drawing.
wrong.move: counts the squares inside a shape on squared paper when asked how far it is round the edge, giving five for a shape whose boundary is twelve.
wrong.screen: the walker goes round the outside one square's edge at a time, each edge lighting amber as the sum climbs to twelve, while the five squares inside are lit green and left alone. The child's five stays in the slot beside the green squares, and the twelve stands beside the amber edge.

phases.screen: a rectangle with two of its sides labelled, the walker at one corner and the sum empty
phases.soWhat: The perimeter is the length all the way round, every side of the boundary added once.

phases.win: the adding and the times-four answer land side by side on the same number
phases.does: walks the square once, adding, then presses times four and compares
phases.goal: a figure with four equal sides has a perimeter of four times its side
phases.says: Add the four sides. Now try four times one side. Is it the same?
phases.check: A square has sides of seven centimetres. Find its perimeter by adding, then by four times the side. Do they agree?
phases.feels: four equal sides is one side said four times
phases.hands: Draw a square of side six on squared paper. Walk a finger round it, adding six at each side. Ask how many sixes were added, and write four sixes beside the sum. Then ask whether four times one side works for a rectangle that is not a square, and let the class find that it does not, because its sides are not all equal.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how long is each side of the square? Second rung, the phase's: how many sides does the walker cross to get home? Third rung: the square is cut to a side of two, and the walker's four steps are written out as twos beside the times-four key. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a rectangle is described by two numbers, a length and a breadth, and two sounds like the right count of sides to use.
wrong.move: gives a square's perimeter as its side times two, writing eighteen for a tile of side nine.
wrong.screen: the walker walks the square side by side, each nine dropping into the sum, and it stands at eighteen with the walker only half way round, at the opposite corner. It walks on and the sum climbs to thirty-six as it gets home, and the times-four key writes four nines beside it. The child's eighteen stays in the slot beside the half way mark.

wrong.why: four belongs with a square, and adding it is the quickest thing to do with a four.
wrong.move: adds four to the side instead of multiplying by four, writing thirteen for a square of side nine.
wrong.screen: the times-four key shows its adding: nine, and nine, and nine, and nine, written one under another beside the square's four sides, each side lighting as its nine is written. Nine and four is written beside the stack, one side and a little more, and both stay drawn with the child's answer in the slot.

phases.screen: a square with one side labelled and the times-four key waiting
phases.soWhat: A square's four sides are equal, so its perimeter is four times its side.

phases.win: the missing length drops onto the side, the walker walks on, and the sum takes all six sides
phases.does: opens the facing-sides bracket, reads the missing length off, then lets the walker finish
phases.goal: every side belongs to the perimeter, and a side with no label is found from the sides facing it
phases.says: This side has no label. Which sides face it? Stack them and find it.
phases.check: An L-shape has a left side of eleven and a bottom of nine. From the top, go across five, down a side with no label, across four and down seven. How long is the missing side?
phases.feels: a side with no number on it is still a side, and the sides facing it know how long it is
phases.hands: Cut an L-shape out of card with every corner square, and label every side but one upright side. Stand the short upright pieces on one side against the long upright side facing them, with a ruler laid across the steps, and ask what the unlabelled piece must be. Then do the same across. Point out that the exercise's own fully labelled U-shape and upside-down T close up this way across, their pieces along the top adding up to the bottom.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which side has no label? Second rung, the phase's: which sides run the same way as it, and which long side faces them? Third rung: the figure is cut to an L with small whole sides, and the bracket stacks the short sides against the long one before the child reads the gap. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the numbers printed on a figure look like the whole list of its sides, and the exercise's own L-shape gives forty-five this way when its perimeter is fifty-two.
wrong.move: adds only the printed numbers on the L-shape and stops, giving twenty-nine for a boundary of thirty-four.
wrong.screen: the walker stops at the side with no label and will not step along it; the sum holds at the sides already walked, and the unlabelled side stays lit with its empty label box. The facing-sides bracket opens and lays the three and the empty side end to end above the eight they face, and the missing five is read off the space left. Only then does the walker go on, and the sum reaches thirty-four beside the child's twenty-nine, both standing.

wrong.why: the bracket's rule is to take short sides from the long side facing them, and nine and six are a long side and a short side sitting right there on the figure.
wrong.move: takes the missing upright side from sides that run across, writing three, which is nine less six.
wrong.screen: the missing side is lit, upright, and the bracket lights only the sides that run the same way as it, the upright three on the right and the eight on the left facing it, while the sides running across dim. Laid end to end above the eight, the upright three and the empty bar leave a space of five. The child's three stays in the slot, and the sides across are then stacked on their own to show three and six making nine, a true fact about a different pair of sides.

phases.screen: an L-shape with every side labelled but one upright side, the walker stopped beside it
phases.soWhat: Every side belongs to the perimeter, labelled or not; on a stepped shape, the short sides along one side add up to the long side facing them.
phases.concept: A side with no label still counts

phases.win: one length is left in the bay, it slides onto the blank side, and the walker's sum matches the middle
phases.does: takes each given side off the perimeter in the missing-side bay until one length is left
phases.goal: a missing side is the perimeter less every side that is given
phases.says: The whole way round is written in the middle. Take off the sides you can see.
phases.check: A triangle has a perimeter of thirty centimetres and two sides of twelve and eight. What is the third side?
phases.feels: the whole way round is known, so the missing piece is whatever the others leave
phases.hands: Write a perimeter in the middle of a four-sided figure drawn on the board, and label three of its sides. Cut a strip of paper as long as the perimeter and tear off a piece as long as each given side, one at a time. Ask what the last piece is, and hold it against the blank side.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is written in the middle? Second rung, the phase's: what do the given sides add up to? Third rung: the figure is cut to a triangle with a small perimeter, and the bay takes off one given side at a time with the length left written after each. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every perimeter so far has been found by adding, and adding is what the numbers round a boundary seem to be for.
wrong.move: adds the given sides to the perimeter instead of taking them away, writing eighty-seven for a field of fifty.
wrong.screen: the bay lays the perimeter as one long bar of fifty and lays the three given sides along it end to end, ten, fifteen and twelve, leaving a gap at the end that measures thirteen. The child's eighty-seven is drawn as a bar beside it, far longer than the whole boundary, and both stay drawn, nothing marked.

wrong.why: one side is missing and one side is taken away, which sounds like a fair swap.
wrong.move: takes away only one of the given sides, writing forty for a field whose other two sides were given too.
wrong.screen: the forty is slid onto the blank side and the walker walks the whole boundary: ten, fifteen, twelve and forty make seventy-seven, and the fifty written in the middle stands unmatched beside the sum. The bay then takes off the other two given sides one at a time, and the length left shrinks to thirteen, with the child's forty still in the slot.

phases.screen: a figure with its perimeter written in the middle and one side left blank
phases.soWhat: A missing side is the perimeter less every side that is given.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the bracket closes on the side with no label. The short sides lift off the figure as amber bars and lay themselves end to end, the long side facing them lies down in the row beneath, and the empty bar at the end of the top row stretches until its end sits exactly over the end of the long bar, where it stops by itself with its length written in. Then it flies back to the figure and drops onto the unlabelled side, and the walker, which has been waiting there, steps along it and on round to home. It can be replayed as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a rectangle lies on the board with two sides labelled, its length and its breadth, the walker standing at its lower left corner and the sum empty. On the second a square lies with one side labelled and the times-four key drawn unlit below the board. On the third an L-shape lies with every side labelled but one upright side, the walker already stopped at the top of that side and the facing-sides bracket folded shut beside the board. On the fourth a four-sided figure lies with its perimeter written in its middle, three sides labelled and the fourth blank, and the missing-side bay open at the right. The running count at the top left holds the sum, empty, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the walker, or the times-four key, or the empty label on the unlabelled side, or the perimeter in the middle, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how far it is all the way round. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any figure on the board, labelled or not, with the walker, the string, the facing-sides bracket and the missing-side bay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on adding every side, squares and triangles whose sides are all equal, stepped shapes with a side left unlabelled, and a missing side from the perimeter.
voiceLines: A figure with its sides labelled and a walker at one corner. How far is it all the way round?
Walk all the way round. Add each side as you go. Does the string agree?
Add the four sides. Now try four times one side. Is it the same?
This side has no label. Which sides face it? Stack them and find it.
The whole way round is written in the middle. Take off the sides you can see.
A new figure. Count its sides before the walker sets off.
Free play. Any figure, labelled or not, with the walker, the string and the bracket open.
Walk it again from the same corner, and say each side as you add it.
Every side walked once, every missing side found, and every sum matching the string.

observations.why: Walking round adds each side once, and the string is those same sides laid end to end.
observations.soWhat: The perimeter is one length, the whole boundary, however it is measured.
observations.observe: The walker's sum and the straightened string reached the same mark on the ruler.

observations.why: A square's four sides are equal, so adding them is adding one length four times.
observations.soWhat: A square's perimeter is four times its side, and the shortcut works because the four sides are equal.
observations.observe: The times-four key and the walker's adding landed on the same number for every square.

observations.why: On a stepped shape the short sides along one side reach exactly as far as the long side facing them, because the figure closes up.
observations.soWhat: Every side counts, labelled or not, and on a stepped shape a missing side is found from the sides facing it.
observations.observe: The walker would not go on at the side with no label, and the bracket found it from the sides facing it.

observations.why: The perimeter is all the sides together, so whatever the given sides do not cover is the one that is missing.
observations.soWhat: A missing side is the perimeter less every side that is given.
observations.observe: Taking the given sides off the perimeter left exactly the blank side's length.

description: Walk round a figure side by side adding every length, find a side with no label from the sides facing it, and find a missing side from the perimeter.

serves.exercise: finding the perimeter of a rectangle from its length and breadth
finding the perimeter of each of six figures, one of them with a side left unlabelled
finding the missing side of four figures from the perimeter written inside each
finding the perimeters of five figures drawn on squared paper

source_tool.description: A figure lies on the stage with its sides labelled in centimetres, and a small walker stands at one corner. Each tap sends the walker along one side, and the side's length drops into a running sum at the top left of the canvas, so every side is added once and none twice; when the walker gets home, the sum is the perimeter. A string control lays a string tight round the whole boundary, lifts it off and straightens it against a ruler, so the perimeter is seen as one length. Labelling one side of a rectangle lights the side opposite it with the same length. A times-four key works only on a figure whose four sides are all equal, and shows the adding it replaces. When the walker reaches a side with no label it stops, and it will not go on until that side is found: a facing-sides bracket lights the sides on one side of the stepped shape that run the same way as the missing one, and the side facing them, and stacks them beside each other so the missing piece can be read off as the difference. A missing-side bay runs the other way: the perimeter is written in the middle, the given sides are taken off one by one, and what is left is the side that was missing.
source_tool.art_direction: A walker round a labelled figure / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Walk it again from the same corner, and say each side as you add it.
voice.onNext: A new figure. Count its sides before the walker sets off.
voice.opening: A figure with its sides labelled and a walker at one corner. How far is it all the way round?
voice.onFinish: Every side walked once, every missing side found, and every sum matching the string.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any figure, labelled or not, with the walker, the string and the bracket open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A side with no label still counts

placement.where: After a desk, a book and a window pane have been measured side by side and a string laid round each. The tool is what stops the walker at a side with no label and will not add the next side until it is found, which a list of numbers on paper never does.

answer_key.rule: The perimeter is the total length of the boundary, found by adding the lengths of all the sides. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so its perimeter is its length and its breadth added twice. All four sides of a square are equal, so its perimeter is four times its side, and a triangle with all three sides equal has its one side added three times. Every side belongs to the perimeter whether it is labelled or not. In a stepped shape, the sides running one way along one side add up to the side facing them, so a missing side is that facing side less the others beside it. When the perimeter is given, a missing side is the perimeter less all the sides that are given.
answer_key.wrong: The walker goes round again one side at a time from the same corner, with each length dropping into the sum as it is walked, and the facing sides are stacked beside each other again. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so the frame has two sides of twenty-five and two of fifteen.
Walk round adding each side once: twenty-five, fifteen, twenty-five and fifteen.
That makes eighty centimetres, which is the frame's perimeter.
items.question: A photo frame is twenty-five centimetres long and fifteen centimetres wide. How far is it all the way round?
items.checkpoint: The perimeter is every side of the boundary added once.
items.misconception: Adding only the two sides that are labelled, which gives forty, half the perimeter.

steps: All four sides of a square are equal, so every side is nine centimetres.
Adding them gives nine, nine, nine and nine, which is thirty-six.
Four times nine is also thirty-six, so the quick way and the adding agree.
items.question: A square tile has sides of nine centimetres. What is its perimeter?
items.checkpoint: The perimeter of a square is four times its side.
items.misconception: Giving the side, nine, or multiplying by two instead of four.

steps: The upright sides on the right, the unlabelled one and the three, face the left side of eight.
So together they make eight, and the missing side is eight less three, which is five.
Now add all six sides: eight, three, five, six, three and nine make thirty-four centimetres.
items.answer: Thirty-four centimetres; the side with no label is five centimetres
items.question: An L-shape has a left side of eight centimetres. From its top, go across three, down a side with no label, across six and down three. Then go back along the bottom, nine. Find the perimeter.
items.checkpoint: Every side belongs to the perimeter, and a side with no label is found from the sides facing it.
items.misconception: Adding only the printed numbers, which gives twenty-nine and leaves a whole side out.

steps: The perimeter is all four sides added, so the three given sides and the missing one make fifty.
The three given sides, ten, fifteen and twelve, add up to thirty-seven.
Fifty less thirty-seven is thirteen, so the fourth side is thirteen metres.
items.question: A four-sided field has a perimeter of fifty metres. Three of its sides are ten, fifteen and twelve metres. How long is the fourth side?
items.checkpoint: A missing side is the perimeter less every side that is given.
items.misconception: Adding the perimeter to the given sides, or taking away only one of them.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A triangle has sides of four, six and seven centimetres. Find its perimeter.
A rectangular mat is sixty centimetres long, and its width is half its length. Find its perimeter.
items.final_answer: One hundred eighty centimetres: the width is thirty, and sixty, thirty, sixty and thirty make one hundred eighty

items.question: A square has sides of twelve centimetres. What is its perimeter?
An equilateral triangle, a triangle with all three sides equal, has sides of eight centimetres. What is its perimeter?
items.final_answer: Twenty-four centimetres, eight added three times

items.question: An L-shape has a left side of thirteen centimetres and a bottom of ten. From the top of the left side, go across four, down a side with no label, across six and down eight. Find the missing side and the perimeter.
items.final_answer: The missing side is five, because it and the eight face the thirteen. The perimeter is forty-six centimetres

items.question: A staircase shape has a left side of ten centimetres and a bottom of nine. From the top, it steps down to the right: across two, down four, across three, down a step with no label, across four, and down two. Find the missing step and the perimeter.
items.final_answer: The missing step is four, because four, the missing step and two face the ten. The perimeter is thirty-eight centimetres

items.question: A triangle has a perimeter of twenty-seven centimetres. Two of its sides are nine and eleven centimetres. Find the third side.
items.final_answer: Seven centimetres, because twenty-seven less twenty is seven

items.question: A rectangle has a perimeter of forty centimetres. Three of its sides are fourteen, six and fourteen centimetres. How long is the fourth side?
items.final_answer: Six centimetres, the same as the side opposite it, because forty less thirty-four is six

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: walks one side per tap and adds its length to the sum
adds each walked side at the top left of the canvas
lays a string round the boundary and straightens it against a ruler
lights the side opposite a labelled side of a rectangle
multiplies the side of a figure with four equal sides, showing the adding it replaces
stacks the sides running one way along one side beside the side facing them
takes the given sides off a given perimeter one by one

teaching_notes: Measure something real before the tool is opened, a desk or a book, and lay a string round it too, so the class sees the perimeter as one length before it becomes a sum. Then use the walker, because it adds every side once and cannot skip one. The worked triangle on the page is drawn with a square corner and labelled six, seven and eight centimetres, which no triangle with a square corner can be; its perimeter, twenty-one, is still right, so use the numbers and not the drawing. The one figure that needs real care is the L-shape with a side left unlabelled. Adding the printed numbers gives forty-five, and the perimeter is fifty-two. The page never shows how to find such a side, but its own fully labelled stepped figures show the rule, and this tool teaches only that: the sides running one way along one side of a stepped shape add up to the side facing them, across and upright alike. When the exercise says equilateral, say what it means, a triangle with all three sides equal, because the chapter never does. The Critical Thinking cloth asks for a perimeter and not an area; halve the length to get the width first.
generation_prompt: Build a perimeter tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A figure lies in the working area with its sides labelled in centimetres and drawn to scale with those labels, and a small walker stands at one corner. Each tap moves the walker along one side and drops that side's length into a running sum at the top left of the canvas, so each side is added exactly once. A string control lays a string tight round the whole boundary, lifts it off and straightens it along a ruler. Labelling one side of a rectangle lights the side opposite it with the same length. A times-four key appears only for a figure with four equal sides, showing the repeated adding beside the product; the chapter gives no such shortcut for any other shape. When the walker reaches a side with no label it stops; a facing-sides bracket then lights the sides on one side of the stepped shape that run the same way as the missing one, and the side facing them, and stacks them next to each other, so the missing length is read off as the difference, and only then does the walker go on. A missing-side bay takes a perimeter written in the middle of a figure and removes the given sides one at a time until one length is left, which slides onto the blank side. Stepped shapes close up exactly, and any triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Walk round the figure one side at a time. Add each side as you go. If a side has no label, find it from the sides facing it. Every side counts. For a missing side, take the other sides off the perimeter.
